slides.text: I lost my hearing entirely when I was twelve, but I never stopped deeply loving music. I would sit at the back of the city's grand symphony hall, pressing my bare hands flat against the wooden floorboards just to feel the heavy vibrations of the orchestra. For months, the lead cellist, a handsome man with intense dark eyes, would watch me from the stage, utterly puzzled by my strange, silent ritual.

One evening after a grueling rehearsal, the concert hall was completely empty. As I pressed my hands to the floor, I felt a new, distinct vibration. Footsteps. The cellist walked down the long aisle and sat directly beside me on the dusty floor. Without a single word, he took my small hands in his and gently placed them flat against the warm, polished wood of his beautiful, antique cello.

He closed his eyes and began to play. The music surged violently through my fingertips, vibrating deep into my chest and wrapping tightly around my heart. It was the most beautiful thing I had ever felt. When he finished, I looked up, tears streaming down my face. He smiled gently, lifting his hands to clumsily sign the words he had spent weeks practicing just for me: 'May I play for you forever?'
